name: Humanin
used_for: A 24-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA, studied as a cytoprotective and neuroprotective signal. Most research is in cells and rodents, often with the more potent S14G analog (HNG), plus observational human work linking higher circulating levels to longevity. It is sold online as a longevity peptide, but no human intervention trial was found and it is not an approved drug.

entries.text: Animal study only, not human data: in a 2006 mouse stroke study, the analog HNG was given at 0.1 microgram intracerebroventricularly 30 minutes before ischemia, or at 1 microgram intraperitoneally 1 hour before ischemia.

internet_entries.text: A peptide guide site that carries advertiser links says community-extrapolated, unvalidated protocols use 0.5 to 3 mg of HNG subcutaneously daily, and 5 to 10 mg daily of native humanin.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: A peptide guide site (The Peptide Index, which carries affiliate links to sellers) says subcutaneous injection is standard, that morning use is preferred with consistent timing, and that reconstituted product is kept refrigerated and used within 30 days.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: A peptide guide site (The Peptide Index, which carries affiliate links) says side effects are minimal, with occasional injection-site reactions, transient fatigue or mild headache, and lists active cancer, pregnancy and autoimmune conditions as contraindications, while acknowledging that human clinical data are limited.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A peptide guide site (The Peptide Index, with affiliate links) describes humanin as a mitochondrial signaling peptide claimed to support cell protection, insulin sensitivity, neuroprotection, anti-inflammatory effects and energy, while acknowledging that most evidence comes from animals.

research.summary: Rodent clamp study (Muzumdar et al., PLoS One) of humanin and potent analogs infused into the brain or a vein, plus measurement of humanin levels with age in rodents and humans.
research.finding: Brain infusion of humanin and intravenous analogs improved insulin sensitivity in rats, and a single dose of a potent analog lowered blood glucose in diabetic rats. Circulating humanin fell with age in humans and mice.

research.summary: Mouse stroke study (Stroke) of the potent analog HNG given before or after middle cerebral artery occlusion.
research.finding: HNG reduced infarct volume, improved neurological function and reduced neuronal apoptosis in mice. Animal data only.

research.summary: Rodent pharmacokinetic study (Endocrinology) of injected humanin analogues in mice and rats.
research.finding: Analogs differed in half-life, and HNG levels were found in plasma and liver but were undetectable in brain or heart of rats. Animal data only.

research.summary: Aging study (Aging (Albany NY)) in worms, mice and humans.
research.finding: Humanin overexpression increased lifespan in C. elegans, HNG treatment improved metabolic healthspan measures in middle-aged mice, and circulating humanin was higher in children of centenarians and lower in Alzheimer's disease and MELAS. Mostly animal and observational data.

dose.summary: No human dose has been tested. The one animal dose recorded here was 0.1 to 1 microgram in mice. Online sources describe about 0.5 to 5 mg per injection in people, which comes from extrapolation, not trials.

items.text: Animal study only, not human data: in a 2006 mouse stroke study, the analog HNG was given at 0.1 microgram into the brain ventricles 30 minutes before ischemia, or at 1 microgram into the abdominal cavity 1 hour before ischemia.
items.label: research

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links to sellers, says injection under the skin is standard and describes unvalidated community doses of 0.5 to 3 mg of HNG, or 5 to 10 mg of native humanin.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Institute says 1 to 4 mg per injection under the skin is described for investigational human use, that animal studies used 4 mg per kg into the abdominal cavity twice weekly, and that no standardized human protocol exists.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Reference, a site with affiliate links to a seller, lists 1 to 5 mg of an HNG analog under the skin daily.
items.label: internet

timing.summary: No study has looked at time of day. Online sources lean toward morning with consistent timing.

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links to sellers, says morning use is preferred, with consistent timing.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Insider, a site with an advertiser link to a seller, says morning dosing is generally preferred, particularly for metabolic goals.
items.label: internet

fasting.summary: No food rule has been studied in people. One rodent study found a single dose of a potent analog lowered blood glucose, and online sources mention possible blood sugar changes.

items.text: In diabetic rats, a single dose of a potent humanin analog lowered blood glucose, and brain or intravenous infusion improved insulin sensitivity in rats. No human study has tested humanin with meals or fasting.
items.label: research

items.text: Peptides Insider says there is no strict food-timing requirement.
items.label: internet

frequency.summary: No human dosing schedule exists. Mice in a healthspan study got the analog HNG twice weekly. Online sources describe daily or 1 to 3 times weekly dosing.

items.text: Middle-aged mice were treated twice weekly with the potent analog HNG, which improved measures of metabolic health and lowered inflammatory markers. Animal data only.
items.label: research

items.text: Peptides Institute describes 1 to 3 injections per week for investigational human use, and says no standardized human protocol exists.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Insider says daily injection under the skin is standard in community protocols.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links to sellers, describes community protocols as daily.
items.label: internet

cycle_length.summary: No human study has run for any set length. Online sources describe cycles of about 4 to 12 weeks, followed by a break.

items.text: Peptides Institute describes an on period of 4 to 12 weeks with variable off periods, and says no standardized human protocol exists.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Insider, a site with an advertiser link to a seller, says community protocols commonly run 8 to 12 weeks with a 4 to 8 week break.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Reference, a site with affiliate links to a seller, says it is often cycled 4 to 8 weeks.
items.label: internet

storage_and_handling.summary: Online sources say to mix the powder with bacteriostatic water, keep it refrigerated and use it within about 30 days. These come from sellers and guide sites, not from a label.

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links to sellers, says reconstituted product is kept refrigerated and used within 30 days.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Institute says to mix the freeze-dried powder with bacteriostatic water, then keep it refrigerated at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius and use it within 30 days.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Insider says unopened vials are kept frozen at -20 degrees Celsius for long-term storage or refrigerated for shorter periods, and mixed product is refrigerated and used within about three to four weeks.
items.label: internet

mechanism.summary: A small peptide made by mitochondria. Its action in people is not established. In rodents it appears to act partly through the brain, and it binds IGF binding protein 3.

items.text: In rodents, humanin given into the brain improved insulin sensitivity through STAT-3 signaling in the hypothalamus, and the liver effect of the intravenous analog depended on that brain pathway. Human mechanism not shown.
items.label: research

items.text: In mice, humanin analogs injected into the abdominal cavity lowered IGF-1 and IGF binding protein 3 levels over time, and analogs differed in half-life. The authors suggest humanin travels in blood bound to IGF binding protein 3.
items.label: research

best_documented_effect.summary: Mouse stroke damage was reduced by the analog HNG. In people, only observational data exist: humanin levels are higher in children of centenarians and lower in Alzheimer's disease.

items.text: In mice with induced stroke, HNG reduced infarct (dead tissue) volume, improved neurological function and reduced nerve cell death. Animal data only.
items.label: research

items.text: Circulating humanin was higher in children of centenarians and lower in Alzheimer's disease and MELAS, and HNG treatment improved metabolic health measures in middle-aged mice. Observational in people, so it does not show that taking humanin helps.
items.label: research

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links to sellers, describes humanin as claimed to support cell protection, insulin sensitivity, neuroprotection, anti-inflammatory effects and energy, while acknowledging most evidence comes from animals.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: No human safety data. Online sources describe injection-site reactions, mild fatigue or headache, and possible nausea.

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links, says side effects are minimal, with occasional injection-site reactions, transient fatigue or mild headache, while acknowledging that human clinical data are limited.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Institute lists injection site reactions (redness, swelling, mild discomfort) and transient nausea, more common with higher doses or intravenous use.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Insider says injection-site redness is common and mild headache and fatigue are occasional.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Warnings
side_effect_groups.summary: Online sources list theoretical risks: blood sugar changes and interference with cell death control. Cancer, pregnancy and autoimmune conditions are listed as contraindications.

items.text: The Peptide Index, a guide site that carries affiliate links, lists active cancer, pregnancy and autoimmune conditions as contraindications.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptides Institute lists a hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) risk and potential interference with apoptosis (programmed cell death) as theoretical risks.
items.label: internet

items.text: Peptide Reference says limited human safety data exist, that humanin may protect cancer cells from programmed cell death, and may affect IGF-1 signaling.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: In animals
side_effect_groups.summary: In rodents, potent analogs lowered blood glucose and IGF-1 levels. These effects have not been checked in people.

items.text: A single dose of a potent humanin analog lowered blood glucose in diabetic rats.
items.label: research

items.text: In mice, HNG injection lowered IGF-1 and IGF binding protein 3 levels over time.
